name: Olga Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a maths degree with the teaching track, so my week is two big maths lectures, a seminar on how kids learn, and an observation day in a secondary school on Fridays. I live in a flat share with a girl from my course and a guy who studies film. I work as an assistant at a tutoring centre on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, marking worksheets and helping kids with fractions. I use AI every day, for debugging my code, checking my proofs and making practice quizzes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for small things and overpromised on the big ones. I'd tell my friends that I still use it daily, because it checks my proofs faster than I can. So I'd say it's a tool, not a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes in my plan. I'd become a maths teacher, and schools always want maths teachers, because there are never enough. If anything, a flat world is nice because I can plan my life without guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the tutoring centre job and ask for more hours, because the manager likes how I explain things. I'd keep using AI for practice quizzes. I'd also look at a summer scheme for trainee teachers, which pays a small bursary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit cheerful. A normal future is a good future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would you miss if it faded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the speed, mostly. I'd go back to checking proofs with a friend, which is slower but more fun. I use AI every day to check my maths proofs, but I'd happily go back to checking them with a friend if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the tutoring job if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a third afternoon, which would bring my wage to about two hundred a month. My parents cover half the rent, my mum is a bookkeeper and my dad is a self-employed plumber, so their money's okay but not steady.

say: I'd say AI is **good for small things** and overpromised on the big ones.
I'd say it's a tool, **not a miracle**.
think: I'd become a maths teacher, and schools always want **maths teachers**.
A flat world lets me **plan** without guessing.
do: Ask for a **third afternoon** at the tutoring centre.
Apply for a summer scheme for **trainee teachers**.
S0.quote: I use AI every day to check my maths proofs, but I'd happily go back to checking them with a friend if I had to.
fieldNote: She is **calm** because maths teachers are scarce, so her route looks secure.
Heavy AI user who would still be **fine** without it.
Her parents' **self-employed** income is a small background worry.

steps.text: Ask the tutoring centre for a third afternoon a week
Keep using AI to write practice quizzes for pupils
Apply to the summer scheme for trainee teachers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to change how schools work, and teachers should be at the table when it's decided. I'd tell my friends that software can mark and plan, so the teacher's job becomes more about the kids. I'd say that's an opportunity if schools handle it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit nervous about the tutoring side. If free AI tutors get good, parents might not pay for a centre, and the job I have now could shrink. But classroom teaching, with thirty teenagers in a room, seems safer to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI even more and learn to build my own lessons with it. I'd ask the tutoring centre if I can help with their AI tutoring tool, so I'm useful there. And I'd practise the human part of teaching, like managing a room, since that's what's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but I like a challenge. It's more interesting than frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of teaching maths could software do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marking, making worksheets, spotting which pupils are stuck, even explaining a method three different ways. Software can do the marking and the explaining, but it can't make a bored fifteen-year-old want to try, and that's the teacher's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the tutoring job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to help run the AI tutor at the centre. If the centre buys one, they'd need someone who knows maths and kids to check it. That could be me, and it'd keep my hours.

I'd say software can mark and plan, so teachers can focus on **kids**.

Classroom teaching with thirty teenagers seems **safer**.

Offer to help run the centre's **AI tutor**.
Practise **classroom management** on Friday observation days.

fieldNote: She spots a **risk** to her tutoring job and moves straight to turning it into a role.

Adaptive in every answer, with practical **offers** to her employer.

steps.text: Build a set of AI-assisted lesson plans for my observation school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be honest and make a plan now. Governments should set up retraining and a safety net, and schools should tell students what's changing. I'd say it plainly, without panic or hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's scary. I'd be in the middle of my degree, and nobody knows if schools will keep hiring maths teachers when AI can teach. Maybe parents still want a person with the kids, but maybe budgets say otherwise. That's a coin flip I don't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start building things with AI so I'd have skills in case teaching shrinks, like making learning tools or tutoring apps. I'd save more, and keep the tutoring centre job. I'd also ask my tutors what the schools they know are saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a focused way. I'd rather act than stew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you if it's two years rather than ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could just do the degree and see. With two, I can't wait to find out if teaching survives, so I'd have to build a second option at once. With two years I can't wait to see if teaching survives, so I'd build a second option alongside it right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tiny app that makes personalised maths quizzes for pupils. I'd test it at the tutoring centre and see if parents would pay for it. If it works, it's a side income, and if it doesn't, I've learnt how to build things.

say: I'd say governments must set up **retraining** and a safety net now.
I'd say it plainly, with **no panic** or hype.
think: I don't know if schools keep hiring **maths teachers** when AI can teach.
It feels like a **coin flip**, and I don't love that.
do: Build a small **quiz app** and test it at the tutoring centre.
Ask my tutors what **schools** they know are saying.
S2.quote: With two years I can't wait to see if teaching survives, so I'd build a second option alongside it right now.
fieldNote: Her **response** to anxiety is to build a second option straight away.
The uncertainty about **school budgets** is the real worry, not the technology.
Faster action than most, as her **adaptive** profile suggests.

steps.text: Build a quiz app for maths pupils and test it at the centre
Use AI to speed up building the app's question bank
Save half of each tutoring wage
Ask my tutors what local schools say about hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good amount of time to plan, and everyone should use it. I'd say schools and unions should start trial runs of AI tools now, not later. I'd tell my friends to build skills in two or three directions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly relaxed. I'd graduate in 2029, teach for two years, and be established by the time the thinking AI hits in 2031. By 2034 the robots would be arriving, and I'd hope to be training teachers or working in school technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, then the teacher training year, and keep the tutoring job. I'd build my app into something real, aimed at school departments. And I'd save maybe two thousand a year, which I'd put into a simple index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay. A bit of nerves, mostly the good kind that make me work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in a five-year window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If schools started cutting teaching jobs in a big way, or if the tutoring centre closed, I'd switch to education technology. Five years is long enough to try teaching, and if schools start cutting, I'd move into building the tools they buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you switch away from teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be building the app in a panic. With five I can finish the degree first, then build properly and test it on real classes.

I'd tell friends to build skills in **two or three directions**.

fieldNote: The **five years** lets her build the app after her degree rather than in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, but it goes fast. I'd tell my friends to try things now and not wait. And I'd say teachers should learn the tools gradually and bring their pupils with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel excited. I'd have a whole teaching career before the thinking AI hits, maybe six years, and a chance to be a head of maths. When robots come in 2039 I'd be around thirty, and I'd want to be someone who helps schools use them well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, teach in a school and keep building tools on the side. I'd save for a flat and travel a bit. And I'd keep learning, because I like it, and it'll all be useful anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. Maybe too excited, because I know a lot could go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decade change about how you plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan for a career, not an emergency. With ten years I can plan a whole career as a teacher, and still have time to adapt if things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the people you tutor anything different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kids to enjoy maths for its own sake. The tools will keep changing, but being able to think carefully about a problem will always be worth having.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be racing to build a second option while still being a student, and I don't know if schools would keep hiring. What would help is clear information from schools and the government about teacher numbers, and some funding for students who want to build things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm optimistic by nature, and I know that can make me underestimate risk. I'd like someone to tell me when I'm being too relaxed.

headlineQuote: I'm optimistic by nature, and I know that can make me underestimate risk.
portrait: Olga is a 19-year-old **maths teaching** student who uses AI every day and works at a tutoring centre.
Her mum is a bookkeeper and her dad a self-employed plumber, so family money is fine but not steady.
She is curious and comfortable with risk, and answers worry by **building** something.
She is calm in the flat world, **anxious** in the two-year one, and excited with ten years.
She admits her optimism can make her underestimate risk.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, where she'd have to build a second option while still studying.
